title: Master Class | French Defense, Steinitz | Chess Speedrun | Grandmaster Naroditsky
openingName: French Defense: Advance Variation, Steinitz gambit line (4.Nf3)

moves.spoken: Black meets e4 with the pawn to e6 — the French. The plan today is aggressive: build toward the enemy king and see if the attack can land a checkmate.
moves.teaches: The French invites a fight where White can play for a direct kingside attack.
moves.plans: Clamp the centre and hunt the king.

moves.spoken: The pawn goes to e5 — the Advance. This is the Steinitz treatment, a line that has been around forever but flies under the radar: the e5-pawn locks Black in and the whole game will orbit around keeping it there.
moves.teaches: In the Advance French, the e5-pawn is the clamp — everything supports it.
moves.plans: Advance e5 and build around the clamp.

moves.spoken: Black strikes with the pawn to c5, and here everyone and their brother plays c3 to shore up d4. Not today — giving that pawn away looks unthinkable, and that's exactly the point of the line.
moves.teaches: The gambit idea: don't reflexively defend d4 — the initiative can be worth the pawn.

moves.spoken: Pretend nothing is happening and develop the knight to f3. The d4-pawn can fall; what matters is the e5-pawn and a fast, harmonious setup behind it.
moves.teaches: Prioritise the clamping pawn and development over a materially even but passive c3.
moves.plans: Develop; let d4 go if it must.

moves.spoken: Bishop to d3, still developing as if the centre weren't on fire — and quietly inviting Black to grab the pawn. Let him: the e5-pawn is the one really squeezing his position, so that's the pawn to nurse.
moves.teaches: Trade a defended pawn's tension for lead in development; keep the pawn that cramps the opponent.

moves.spoken: Castle and accelerate — the rook is coming to e1 not to attack yet but to over-protect e5. Leave d4 alone, pile support behind the clamp, and let development do the talking.
moves.teaches: Over-protection: heap defenders on your key pawn so it can never be undermined.

moves.spoken: The knight to h6 is the standard French rerouting — it's heading for f5. Don't capture it; taking only helps Black's structure and hands him the open lines he wants.
moves.teaches: Don't grab a knight bound for a good square if the recapture repairs the opponent's position.

moves.spoken: The knight to c3 — looking deeper, this stops the ...Nb4-d6 idea that would dig at the light bishop, and it develops toward the centre. Sometimes the useful move is simply the one that denies the opponent his plan.
moves.teaches: A developing move that also prevents the opponent's regrouping is doubly valuable.

moves.spoken: Here is the move to burn into memory: with a knight on c3 and the enemy queen on b6, always look at the knight to a4. It hits the queen and the c5-pawn at once, and Black's whole queenside starts to wobble.
moves.teaches: Nc3 + enemy queen on b6 is a standing cue: Na4 forks the queen and c5.
moves.plans: Na4, win the tempo and the c5 tension.

moves.spoken: The knight takes on c5 and the bishop recaptures — and that's the real gain. When the dust settles Black's dark-squared bishop has been traded off, White owns the two bishops, and Black's position is positionally in shambles.
moves.teaches: Trading a knight to eliminate a key bishop can be a positional win — the bishop pair is the prize.
moves.plans: Win the bishop pair, then press.

moves.spoken: No rush to attack — the pawn to c3 guards the d4-square, a very typical, solid touch, and Black's ...Ng4 is nothing to fear because the queen to e2 and a later h3 simply shove it back. Play it positionally first.
moves.teaches: Consolidate a key square before attacking; a harmless knight sortie is met by kicking it away.

moves.spoken: The pawn to b4 isn't just a hit on the queen — it stakes out c5 as an outpost. Every tempo now buys an important square for the pieces, and the bishop already has its eye on that hole.
moves.teaches: Gain a tempo AND a square in one move — attacking with purpose, not just for the check.

moves.spoken: The bishop swings to d6, parking itself right in Black's gut and slicing down the diagonal. There was no hurry — but with everything else in place, planting it here is a fine way to finish the buildup.
moves.teaches: Post a bishop on a dominant central square once the rest of the setup is complete.
moves.plans: Bd6, then switch to the kingside.

moves.spoken: Now for the concrete phase. Development is done, the bishop dominates, and Black's king is stuck in the centre with no castling in sight — so the knight jumps to g5 and the queen heads for h5. This is going for the throat.
moves.teaches: Only launch the direct attack once development is complete and the enemy king is fixed.
moves.plans: Ng5, Qh5, mate the stranded king.

moves.spoken: In hindsight, Black defended the opening well; the trouble started with the queen chased to a7 and the tilt that followed — the slow ...Ng8 and the weakening ...b6-b4 ideas. Against a fixed king, those concessions add up fast.
moves.teaches: One provoked retreat can start a slide; slow, weakening moves against an attack compound quickly.
